title: Funding Clinical Trials and Overseas R&D Activities
excerpt: Accessing the R&D Tax Incentive as a biotechnology or medical technology company is rarely as straightforward as it is for other sectors.

blocks.text: Accessing the R&D Tax Incentive as a biotechnology or medical technology company is rarely as straightforward as it is for other sectors. Two areas consistently create uncertainty: clinical trials and overseas R&D activities. In our experience, many businesses are aware these activities can be eligible but misunderstand the conditions that determine whether expenditure can ultimately be claimed.
At GrantReady, our team knows these pathways well and can help you maximise your funding while you continue to innovate.

If you haven't already, start with the fundamentals of [R&D Tax Incentive eligibility](#rdti): the turnover, spend and activity tests every claim must meet. This article covers what's different when your R&D involves clinical trials or work done outside Australia.
Clinical Trials: What's Actually Eligible

Clinical trials may be eligible under the R&D Tax Incentive, subject to the conditions in the Industry Research and Development (Clinical Trials) Determination 2022. Trials conducted to develop an unapproved therapeutic good can be eligible across these stages:

items: Phase 0 and Phase I trials
Phase II and Phase III trials
Pre-market pilot stage trials
Pre-market pivotal stage trials

blocks.text: Eligibility is subject to further exclusions set out in the Determination, meaning the design, purpose and regulatory context of a trial can be just as important as its phase.
Advance and Overseas Finding: Claiming R&D Conducted Outside Australia

Unlike many industries, biotechnology and medical technology companies often need access to a particular patient population, specialised overseas facilities, or research partners with expertise that doesn't exist locally. Overseas activities are therefore relatively common, but companies frequently underestimate the planning needed to secure an Overseas Finding before they claim.

To claim the R&D Tax Incentive for overseas R&D activities, you must apply for and receive a positive Overseas Finding. This application must be lodged before the end of the income year in which the activities are conducted, and the activities must also be separately registered.
To qualify, the overseas activities must be unable to be conducted solely in Australia, for one of four specific reasons:

items: **Facilities, equipment or expertise:** the work required access to specific facilities, equipment or expertise that simply doesn't exist in Australia
**Quarantine laws:** conducting the activities in Australia would have breached Australian quarantine laws
**Access to a specific population:** the work required access to a particular population of living things, for example a specific group of patients or organisms, not available in Australia
**Unique geographical or geological features:** the work required access to a specific landscape, terrain or geological formation that doesn't exist in Australia

blocks.text: Financial reasons alone are not a prescribed condition: lower costs overseas are not, by themselves, enough to show the activity couldn't be conducted in Australia. Read more about how the [Advance and Overseas Finding process](#blog-overseas) works.

items.label: Prescribed reasons an overseas activity can qualify
Refundable offset available on eligible R&D spend
Overseas Finding deadline for R&D activities in the 2026-27 financial year

blocks.text: If you intend to claim overseas R&D expenditure for the 2026-27 financial year, your Overseas Finding application must be lodged before that date. We strongly recommend starting well ahead of the deadline.
Want to discuss how these rules apply to you? [Book a free consultation call](#book-lina) and our team will be happy to help.

title: 2025-26 Deadline: Advance and Overseas Findings
excerpt: You can only claim the R&D Tax Incentive for work done outside Australia if you first obtain a positive Overseas Finding from AusIndustry. Here are the four conditions you must meet.

blocks.text: You can only claim the R&D Tax Incentive for work conducted outside Australia if you first obtain a positive Overseas Finding from AusIndustry. The process is strict, and requires strong evidence that your overseas activities are essential and cannot be conducted solely in Australia.
All four of the following conditions must be met.
1. The overseas activity must be an R&D activity
The overseas activity must meet the R&D Tax Incentive's requirements for either a core R&D activity or a supporting R&D activity.
2. It must be needed to complete an Australian core R&D activity
Your Overseas Finding application needs to show that:

items: there is at least one core R&D activity conducted, or to be conducted, solely in Australia (the Australian core activity), and
you cannot complete the Australian core activity without conducting the overseas R&D activity.

blocks.text: 3. It cannot be conducted solely in Australia
You must show that the overseas activity cannot be conducted solely in Australia, for one of four allowable reasons. Conducting the activity:

items: requires access to a facility, expertise or equipment not available in Australia
would contravene laws relating to quarantine
requires access to a population of living things not available in Australia
requires access to geographical or geological features not available in Australia.

blocks.text: Your application must also provide evidence that you made reasonable efforts to access the required resource within Australia. **Financial reasons alone are not sufficient** to meet this condition.
4. Overseas spend must be less than the related Australian spend

Your application needs to show the total actual and projected expenditure on the related Australian and overseas activities. The total cost of the overseas activities must be less than that of the related Australian core and supporting activities.

title: Federal Budget Update: Proposed Changes to the R&D Tax Incentive
excerpt: The recent Federal Budget included a number of proposed changes to the R&D Tax Incentive program that may affect how businesses claim R&D from 1 July 2028.

blocks.text: The recent Federal Budget included a number of proposed changes to the R&D Tax Incentive that may affect how businesses claim R&D from 1 July 2028.

The proposed reforms appear to adopt several recommendations from the Government's Strategic Examination of Research and Development report, and are intended to reshape how innovation support is delivered in Australia. Here are the key points.
Higher offset for experimental core activities

The Budget proposes an increase of approximately 25–50% to the R&D tax offset for experimental core R&D activities only, to better reward genuinely experimental work. Further detail is expected once exposure draft legislation and ATO guidance are released, likely later in the 2026–27 financial year or into 2027.
No more eligibility for supporting-only expenditure

Under the proposal, expenditure that solely supports R&D activities would no longer be eligible. This is expected to reduce some claims, particularly where supporting activities make up a significant share of total R&D spend. The overall impact will depend on each business's mix of core and supporting expenditure, and may be partly offset by the higher core offset rate.
R&D intensity threshold lowered to 1.5%

The R&D intensity threshold is proposed to fall from 2% to 1.5%, making the higher offset rate easier to reach. This is expected to benefit larger businesses on the non-refundable tier, particularly those previously just below the 2% threshold.
Refundable offset expanded for younger businesses

The turnover threshold for the refundable offset is proposed to rise from $20 million to $50 million, giving more support to young, fast-growing businesses. However, refundability would be limited to businesses operating for less than 10 years; older businesses would receive an equivalent non-refundable offset. This may affect cashflow for established companies that continue to invest heavily in R&D.
Maximum expenditure cap raised to $200 million

The cap on eligible R&D expenditure is proposed to rise from $150 million to $200 million. This targets larger businesses and is intended to encourage more R&D to be done in Australia rather than overseas.
Minimum spend threshold raised to $50,000

The minimum R&D expenditure threshold is proposed to rise from $20,000 to $50,000. Claims below this level would need to be made in conjunction with a Research Service Provider (RSP) or Cooperative Research Centre (CRC). This is softer than the previously suggested $150,000 threshold, and gives some relief to smaller claimants.

title: R&D Tax Incentive 2024-25: Register by 30 April 2026
excerpt: If your company spent at least $20,000 on eligible R&D in 2024–25, you may qualify for a tax offset of up to 43.5% through the R&D Tax Incentive.

blocks.text: If your company spent at least $20,000 on eligible R&D in 2024–25, you may qualify for a tax offset of up to 43.5% through the R&D Tax Incentive. The program supports businesses developing new or improved products, processes or technologies where the outcome was genuinely uncertain.
Who is eligible?
Companies that are:

items: incorporated in Australia, or
incorporated offshore but an Australian income tax resident, or
incorporated offshore in a country with which Australia has a double tax agreement, and carrying on business in Australia through a permanent establishment.

blocks.text: What activities qualify?
Your R&D activities must:

items: aim to create new or improved products, processes or technology
resolve technical uncertainty that could not be solved using existing knowledge
use a systematic approach to experimentation.

blocks.text: A refundable cash benefit
Companies with turnover of less than $20 million may be eligible for a refundable tax offset. That means you could receive a direct cash payment, not just a reduction in tax.
Don't miss the deadline
Registration for the 2024–25 year closes on **30 April 2026**. Missing it may mean waiting another year to claim.
Unsure whether your activities qualify? We can assess your eligibility and guide you through the process. [Book a free consultation call](#book-lina) to make sure you don't miss out.

title: How to Claim Overseas R&D Under the R&D Tax Incentive
excerpt: You can claim the R&D Tax Incentive for work conducted outside Australia, but only if you first obtain a positive Overseas Finding from AusIndustry.

blocks.text: You can claim the R&D Tax Incentive for work conducted outside Australia, but only if you first obtain a positive Overseas Finding from AusIndustry. The process is strict, and requires strong evidence that your overseas activities are essential and cannot reasonably be conducted in Australia.
There are four key requirements, and you must meet all of them.
1. Scientific necessity and activity links
Your overseas activities must:

items: qualify as core or supporting R&D activities
have a direct, scientifically based connection to your Australian core R&D activity
be shown to be necessary to progress the Australian R&D, meaning the Australian activity cannot be completed without the overseas component.

blocks.text: This scientific dependency must be clearly explained in your Overseas Finding application.
2. Unavailability in Australia
You must prove that the activity cannot reasonably be conducted in Australia because of:

items: facilities, equipment, technology or scientific expertise not available locally
specific environmental, geographical or geological conditions found only overseas, or
regulatory restrictions (such as quarantine laws) that prevent the activity from occurring in Australia.

blocks.text: **Note:** financial considerations, such as lower costs overseas, are not a valid justification on their own.
3. Cost balance
The R&D Tax Incentive is designed to prioritise Australian R&D. Your expenditure on overseas R&D activities must therefore be less than your Australian R&D expenditure over the life of the project.
4. Timing and validity
Timing is strict and non-negotiable:

items: Overseas Finding applications must be submitted before the end of the income year in which the activity occurs.
Late applications cannot be accepted, and no extensions, exemptions or discretion apply.
A positive Overseas Finding is valid only for the duration of the approved activity.

blocks.text: After you receive a finding
Even with a positive Overseas Finding, companies must still:

items: register all R&D activities with AusIndustry each year, and
lodge the claim through the company tax return to receive the offset.

title: 2024-25 R&D Tax Incentive Deadline: Five Things to Get Right
excerpt: The 30 April 2026 deadline for the 2024-25 Research and Development Tax Incentive (RDTI) is fast approaching.

blocks.text: The 30 April 2026 deadline for the 2024-25 Research and Development Tax Incentive (RDTI) is fast approaching. If your company invested in innovation during the last financial year (ending 30 June 2025), now is the time to secure your funding.
Here are five things to keep in mind for a successful application.
1. Know the deadline, and the limits of extensions
The statutory registration deadline is 30 April. AusIndustry does allow extensions, but only if you request one before the deadline:

items: **Up to 14 days:** request through the portal before 30 April, with your explanation.
**Up to 92 days:** longer extensions require convincing evidence and are not guaranteed. 92 days beyond the deadline is the legal maximum.

blocks.text: 2. Clearly explain your technical uncertainty

Eligibility doesn't hinge on effort or commercial aims; it hinges on technical uncertainty. Your application must prove the knowledge gap, the hypothesis, and why the outcome could not be determined in advance.

Supporting evidence matters here. Keep the sources you investigated before starting the project to prove the knowledge gap, including records of discussions with competent professionals, along with project plans, design iterations, test results, internal emails, and anything else that shows a genuine, systematic approach to problem-solving.
3. Recheck your eligible R&D expenditure
R&D claims are rarely limited to wages. Depending on your activities, eligible expenditure may also include:

items: contractor and consultant costs
materials consumed during testing
some business overheads
depreciation on assets used for R&D.

blocks.text: 4. Get the application right

AusIndustry's recent application form changes bring a renewed focus on compliance. Weak activity descriptions, unclear hypotheses or copy-and-paste language are more likely to trigger questions, or even an audit. A solid, well-reasoned registration now can save months (sometimes years) of stress later. Starting early gives you time to prepare a robust, defensible application that meets AusIndustry's expectations.
5. Lodge early

The registration portal often slows significantly in the final 48 hours before the deadline, and system failures can occur. Submit early, or request a 14-day extension well before 30 April, to avoid last-minute issues.

title: Ready to Lodge? New AusIndustry Form from 15 August
excerpt: AusIndustry has released a new R&D Tax Incentive application form, effective 15 August. On the surface, the changes may look like small tweaks.

blocks.text: AusIndustry has released a new R&D Tax Incentive application form, effective 15 August. On the surface, the changes may look like small tweaks. In reality, they mark a shift in how applications are assessed, and raise the stakes if you get it wrong.
What's new

items: **More detail required:** larger character limits mean longer, more technical explanations of your projects.
**Additional questions:** covering your documentation and record-keeping.
**Sources investigated:** you'll now need to outline what you reviewed before starting your R&D.

blocks.text: Why it matters

The application is no longer just about registering your R&D activities. The extra information it collects can be used by AusIndustry and the ATO in later compliance reviews. In effect, the form is starting to look like an audit document. That means:

items: **More preparation time and cost:** vague answers won't cut it; detailed, evidence-backed explanations are needed.
**Greater scrutiny:** incomplete or unclear responses could flag your claim for review, even if your activities are otherwise eligible.
**Added compliance burden:** elements of the more detailed Advance Finding process, such as projected expenditure and record-keeping standards, are now part of the registration stage.

blocks.text: Get expert help

That's why expert guidance has never been more important. GrantReady has helped Australian businesses secure more than $700 million in R&D support over the past 20 years. We know how to prepare applications that stand up to scrutiny, without overburdening your business.

title: Northern Territory 2025-26 Budget: Highlights
excerpt: The Northern Territory 2025-26 Budget was handed down on 13 May 2025. Here are some highlights:

blocks.text: The Northern Territory 2025-26 Budget was handed down on 13 May 2025. Here are the highlights for businesses and Territorians.
Cost of living support for businesses

items: Up to $68,750 through the increased payroll tax-free threshold, as well as a payroll tax exemption for wages paid or payable to apprentices and trainees.
Up to $12,000 grant to buy and install batteries and inverters under the Home and Business Battery Scheme.

Around $2,900 for small and $27,000 for large businesses in 2025-26 in electricity subsidies through community service obligation funding to electricity retailers to maintain prices below cost of supply.
Up to $2,500 to buy and install an electric vehicle charger.
Up to $15,000 for security improvements under the Biz Secure program.

blocks.text: Cost of living support for individuals

items: Electricity subsidies through community service obligation funding to retailers, keeping prices below the cost of supply: $1,900 for families, and $1,400 for senior Territorians and apprentices/trainees.
$1,800 for a couple building their first home.
Up to $12,000 grant to buy and install batteries and inverters for families under the Home and Business Battery Scheme.

Up to $1,000 to buy and install an electric vehicle (EV) charger, and up to $1,500 in EV stamp duty concessions on the registration of new and second-hand battery EVs and plug-in hybrid EVs for senior Territorians.
Up to $50,000 to build a new home under the HomeGrown Territory grant.
The FreshStart new home grant of $30,000 to buy or build a new home. In an Australian first, this includes people who have previously owned or currently own a home.

blocks.text: Growing the tourism industry

items: The Territory Government is investing in the tourism sector with funding of $88.4 million in 2025-26 to accelerate tourism growth in the Territory to drive greater interstate and international visitation, economic activity and investment.
The 2025 Budget includes new funding of $8 million per annum from 2025-26 to provide an ongoing sustainable budget for tourism.

The 2025 Budget also includes a $3 million boost to military tourism with an updated Military Heritage Tourism Action Plan. The first stage is the new $1 million Military History Tourism Grant program to help tourism operators develop new military heritage tourism products, expand existing offerings, and enhance visitor experiences.
In addition, government extended the Territory tourism discount scheme and continued the Visitor Experience Enhancement Program.

blocks.text: Building a bigger, better workforce

items: The 2025 Budget includes $120 million for training and higher education to ensure the skill requirements of the Territory economy are met through responsive training and higher education sectors that are aligned to the needs of Territorians and Territory employers.
Further, the 2025 Budget includes additional funding of $2 million per annum in 2025-26 and 2026-27 to attract workers and students to grow the Territory’s population and address workforce shortages.

blocks.text: The full budget papers are available on the [Northern Territory budget website](https://budget.nt.gov.au).

title: 2024-25 Federal Budget: Is There Much New Other Than a Green Bonanza?
excerpt: The 2024-25 Federal Budget delivered a $9.3 billion surplus and billions for green manufacturing, but little new for the rest of business.

blocks.text: Treasurer Jim Chalmers has handed down the 2024-25 Budget, delivering a $9.3 billion surplus with a focus on inflation and cost-of-living pressures. Significant investments aim to make Australia a renewable energy superpower, while the rest of business has largely been ignored.
Green manufacturing

Critical minerals and products essential to the transition to net-zero emissions received a big funding boost. Under its Future Made in Australia plan, the government will direct billions into helping key industries boost local manufacturing and investment, through major loans, investments and incentives. This includes $19.7 billion towards the goal of turning Australia into a renewable energy superpower.

$3.2 billion will be spent over the next decade to accelerate investment in renewable hydrogen, and in solar and battery supply chains. This includes a new innovation fund to support the commercialisation and rollout of renewable technologies, including green metals, low-carbon liquid fuels and battery manufacturing. Battery and solar panel makers are the big beneficiaries, through the $523 million Battery Breakthrough Initiative and the Solar Sunshot program.
$8 billion will be invested over the next decade to support renewable hydrogen production, including a Hydrogen Production Tax Incentive of $2 per kilogram of renewable hydrogen produced from 2027.
Business and jobs
The $20,000 instant asset write-off, due to end on 30 June this year, will be extended for another 12 months. One million eligible small businesses will also benefit from a $325 energy rebate.

The government will also invest $777.4 million to establish the Remote Jobs and Economic Development Program, creating 3,000 jobs in remote Australia and helping income support recipients move into paid work.
Defence

The government will provide $166.2 million to support the Defence Industry Development Strategy. This includes a new Defence Industry Development Grant program, helping Australian businesses increase their scale and competitiveness and respond to Defence capability requirements.
Innovation

The government will invest $46.9 million to support the development of industries in Australia and keep nuclear medicines affordable. This includes $25.9 million for the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation to continue producing affordable nuclear medicines, and $18.0 million to keep building the capability of the National Reconstruction Fund Corporation, building on its 2023–24 establishment.

The government will also provide $1.7 billion over ten years for investments in innovation, science and digital capabilities to support a Future Made in Australia. This spans multiple projects, including:

items: funding for Geoscience Australia to map the nation's groundwater systems and resource endowments, to identify potential discoveries of critical minerals and strategic materials
equity and loans from Export Finance Australia to PsiQuantum Pty Ltd to support the construction and operation of quantum computing capabilities
a new fund for Australia's partnership with the United States on the next generation of the Landsat satellite earth observation program (Landsat Next).

blocks.text: Concerningly, the cost of this measure is being met from savings within the Department of Industry, Science and Resources, highlighting the government's failure to boost investment in innovation.
It's a wrap

The 2024-25 Budget tackles inflation and cost-of-living pressures, but is largely disappointing for business. Green manufacturing, particularly critical minerals and net-zero products, receives substantial funding, and the extended $20,000 instant asset write-off is helpful. However, innovation funding is being met from savings rather than new investment. The Budget prioritises cost of living over new programs for business growth and innovation, except for the green bonanza.
The full budget papers are available on the [Federal budget website](https://budget.gov.au).

title: New Transparency Requirements: ATO to Publish Company Details of R&D Incentive Claimants
excerpt: Since 2020, legislation has required the ATO to publish details of companies that claim the R&D Tax Incentive. Here is what will be published, and when.

blocks.text: To improve transparency within the business community, several new measures were introduced in 2020 into the legislation that governs the R&D Tax Incentive. These include a requirement for the ATO to publish certain details about companies that have claimed the R&D Tax Incentive, and about their claims. The aim is to improve public accountability and encourage voluntary compliance with the program.
What will be published

items: the name of the entity claiming the R&D Tax Incentive
its Australian Business Number (ABN) or Australian Company Number (ACN)
the entity's total R&D expenditure, less any feedstock adjustments.

blocks.text: Publication from September 2024
The ATO will not start publishing details until September 2024, but it has already been contacting claimants and their tax agents to confirm the requirement.

This lead time lets companies check that the information being shared is accurate and up to date, without any immediate impact on their competitive advantage. It is a measured approach that respects the need for businesses to protect sensitive data and their strategic positions.
No additional burden on companies

These transparency requirements do not impose any additional obligations on companies. The ATO recognises that businesses have many concerns and responsibilities to balance, and the measure is designed to provide transparency without adding unnecessary red tape.

While this is new for the R&D Tax Incentive, publishing information about the recipients of government incentives is not. The Federal Government has for many years published details of grant recipients across hundreds of programs, including the recipient, the amount received and a description of the project.

GrantReady supports the government's approach to transparency and recognises its role in building trust and confidence. We will work with our clients to address any concerns as the September 2024 publication date approaches.

title: Australia's Innovation at a Crossroads
excerpt: Australia's R&D spending has fallen to a 17-year low of 1.68% of GDP, well below the OECD average. What does that mean for the nation's innovation future?

blocks.text: Innovation has long been the engine of business progress, and a reflection of Australia's vision for the future. However, recent statistics paint a concerning picture of research and development (R&D) spending in Australia, suggesting the tide of innovation may be receding. While business expenditure on R&D (BERD) rose a commendable 14% in 2021-22, overall investment is falling.
A 17-year low

In August, the Australian Bureau of Statistics revealed that national R&D spending had fallen to 1.68% of GDP in 2021-22: a 17-year low, and down 0.12 percentage points from 2019-20. With R&D spending taking a hit, it's worth looking closely at the numbers and what they mean for Australia's innovation landscape.
Business is still committed to innovation

Of the $38.75 billion spent in 2021-22, businesses contributed $20.6 billion (53%), reflecting their commitment to innovation. The higher education sector contributed $13 billion (34%), with the remainder from government and private not-for-profit organisations. While business R&D spending grew 14% in dollar terms from 2019-20, government spending on R&D hit an all-time low of just 0.49% of GDP in 2022-23.
Looking back over a decade and more, the picture is stark: Australia's R&D expenditure has fallen from a high of 2.4% of GDP in 2008 to 1.68% in 2022.
Below the OECD average

The 1.68% figure is the share of the economy invested in new ideas, breakthrough technologies and the future. A 0.12-point fall from 2019-20 may seem small, but at a 17-year low it sends a clear message about the challenges Australia faces in R&D. It is well below the OECD average of 2.71%, and far behind global leaders such as South Korea at 4.93%.
Does such a small percentage matter?

Strong R&D investment fuels innovation, improves competitiveness and secures a nation's place in a fast-changing global market. As Australia's R&D investment shrinks, there are concerns about its ability to keep pace with other countries. At the 2022 Federal election, Labor pledged to lift R&D expenditure to 3% of GDP by 2030. It's a bold vision, but the current trajectory tells a different story: if spending keeps falling by 0.1% of GDP a year, Australia risks slipping into the lower ranks of OECD countries within five years.
Global standing at risk

The consequences of this downward trend are far-reaching. Industries that rely on innovation to stay competitive may face headwinds, potentially compromising Australia’s global standing in technology, healthcare, and other critical sectors. A decline in R&D spend not only impacts economic growth but also jeopardises the nation’s ability to tackle complex challenges through groundbreaking solutions.
Time to stem the tide

The decline in R&D expenditure should be a wake-up call for policymakers, businesses and the broader Australian community. Business commitment to R&D remains commendable, but a collaborative effort across government, academia and the private sector is needed to reverse the trend. Innovation is the lifeblood of progress, and it's time for Australia to reinvigorate its R&D ecosystem and chart a course towards sustained growth.

title: Made in Victoria: $15M Industry R&D Infrastructure Fund Opens
excerpt: The Victorian Government has announced a $15 million Industry R&D Infrastructure Fund. The Made in Victoria fund is now open for expressions of interest (EOIs) from Victorian businesses.

blocks.text: The Victorian Government has announced a $15 million Industry R&D Infrastructure Fund. The Made in Victoria fund is now open for expressions of interest (EOIs) from Victorian businesses.
A welcome boost
After a period with few large capital grants, this is a welcome boost that Victorian businesses will celebrate.

The program aims to encourage Victorian companies to make new investments in research and development, driving long-term growth and innovation for the State. With matched funding of up to $2 million per project, it supports areas including:

items: new energy technologies, such as wind, hydrogen, solar and batteries
health technologies, including medtech, biotech, pharma and consumer healthcare
food manufacturing and agriculture
defence, aerospace and space
digital and advanced technologies, including advanced materials, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), 3D printing and quantum technologies.

blocks.text: $250,000 to $2 million available
Grants of $250,000 to $2 million (excluding GST) are available for eligible projects on a 1:1 matched funding basis, so up to 50% of eligible project expenditure could be funded.
What is funded?
If your business is planning any of the following, this fund could be the answer:

items: establishing new or expanded R&D infrastructure to deliver process improvements, prototyping, and evaluation and testing of your products and processes
purchasing and commissioning capital equipment (recorded as fixed assets in the applicant's accounting and tax asset registers).

blocks.text: How it fits with the R&D Tax Incentive
The program is designed to complement the Federal Government's R&D Tax Incentive, encouraging Victorian companies to invest in R&D infrastructure in key industry sectors.
Eligibility
To be eligible, a business must operate in Victoria and either employ at least 20 full-time equivalent staff or have an annual turnover between $1.5 million and $100 million.
Closing date
Expressions of interest close on **18 August 2023**, with successful applicants invited to submit a full application in September.
Boosting business

First announced in the 2022-23 Victorian Budget as part of the Victorian Jobs and Investment Fund (VJIF), it's good to see this program now open. Victorian businesses need support for investment and innovation to keep the sector thriving.

title: My R&D Tax Consultant Has Lots of Audit Experience. Should I Be Concerned?
excerpt: If your R&D consultant's work is regularly audited, that's an alarm bell. Here's why, and five tips to stay on the right side of the ATO and AusIndustry.

blocks.text: This is an alarm bell. Great tax consultants shouldn't have their work regularly audited.

Of course, you need a consultant who knows how to handle an audit, because from time to time it does happen. And that's fine: the government is accountable to taxpayers for the money it gives to business.

What you might not know is that the ATO and AusIndustry target consultants they are concerned about. In recent years there has been a crackdown on overly aggressive, inexperienced and incorrect claims. You may have heard about this in the media, and wondered what it means for you.

We asked both the ATO and AusIndustry. They told us they will not go beyond the guidelines; they are simply enforcing them to make sure they only support eligible applicants. That's good news, unless you are doing the wrong thing.
So where does that leave you with your R&D consultant? Can you trust them?
Five tips to stay on the right side of government

items: **Don't be dodgy.** Only claim what you are entitled to, and stay within the legislation.

**Get it right the first time.** Finding out during an audit that you don't have the right information or documentation is a recipe for disaster. It might take more time and effort, but you get peace of mind.
**Know the rules.** Your consultant should be experienced with the legislation, guidelines, case law and history. You can't navigate the maze if you can't read a compass.

**If in doubt, ask.** The government is not the enemy. We work closely with AusIndustry and the ATO, and raise any concerns or questions with them early. They are happy to help, and they really do want you to succeed.

**Get a second opinion.** If you're not sure your consultant is safe, ask for a health check. We do these regularly for companies, free of charge, and it only takes an hour. Some companies are fine while others need help, and we'll always give you an honest opinion so you can put your best foot forward.
